## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. Its default recipe gives only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples each, so too little training may be the main bottleneck, not just the network. To place a brick correctly, the agent has to work out where it lands (the highest filled layer under its footprint) and check that every footprint cell is missing exactly at that layer. The baseline mixes all layers together with 1x1 convolutions, which makes this layer-by-layer check hard to learn. This round tests two things. (1) Recipe: more, smaller updates, fewer PPO epochs (which buys more samples), and a longer horizon for the exact-build bonus. Two recipe variants on the baseline network differ only in ppo_epochs. (2) Architecture: a head that scores each layer separately, then uses a learned softmax gate over layers that can learn to pick the landing layer.

### Round 2
All four results are 0.000 on both seeds, and train success is also 0. That covers the default recipe, recipes trading epochs for samples (1.8–3.1x the default samples), and a per-layer gated head. Recipe changes alone did not help, but every result is zero, so this does not rank the recipes. Either per-step accuracy is far too low to complete any exact build, or the world differs from the description; for example, the anchor or footprint layout may not match the top-left pooling the heads assume. Round 2 tries three structurally different ideas, all on the moderate r1c1-style recipe with entropy 0.01. (1) A head that tolerates layout differences: pooling over each footprint and its transpose, a 3x3 output conv, and the legal-action mask as an input. (2) Column features computed per cell and pooled directly, without being blurred by 3x3 convs first, then a deeper per-type MLP. (3) Global self-attention over cells. Any non-zero result is a meaningful signal.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training, on both seeds. Five quite different networks were tried: pooled footprint heads, per-layer gating, column MLPs, a transformer and a shift-robust head. The recipes also varied: 1 or 2 epochs, 151k to 408k samples, and two entropy values. Results this uniform suggest one shared obstacle rather than a capacity or sample-budget problem. Two candidates fit. First, the action indices may not match the spatial layout the way the description says (for example x-major indexing, flips, or DONE at a different index). The task warns that the world may differ, and a 3x3 offset head would not fix a transpose or a permutation. Second, the policy may collapse to an early DONE, because random placements earn negative reward. This round tests both: a head that learns which of the 8 flips or rotations of the grid maps cells to actions; a general learned remap of all actions; and that remap combined with a stronger exploration and longer-horizon recipe.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored 0 on both seeds, and none had any exact build during training. Recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, smaller batches, higher entropy, longer horizon) did not change this. Neither did head rearrangements meant to fix a possible action-layout mismatch, a transformer trunk, or a column MLP. So the evidence cannot rank anything yet, and the next step is a structural guess.

Two bottlenecks are plausible. First, DONE: an exact build only counts if the agent chooses DONE at exactly the right step. In a flat softmax over about 257 actions, DONE starts near 0.4% and gets crowded out as placement logits sharpen, so the +1 bonus may never be found. Second, landing-layer perception: a good placement needs 'the highest build cell under the footprint is z, and the target is missing at layer z in every footprint cell'. These are per-layer comparisons that 2D trunks blur.

This round therefore tests a separate stop/continue head (on the baseline and on a new per-layer network) and the per-layer network on its own.
